# Configuration reference

Storycreep reads its configuration from environment variables and an optional
configuration file. It validates every key when it starts, and if any key is
missing or invalid it exits with a non-zero status and a message naming each
one. To check a configuration without starting anything, run:

```sh
storycreep validate-config
```

It prints each key's effective value and where the value came from, with
secrets redacted, followed by the capabilities they resolve to.

## Where values come from

For each key, the first of these that is set wins:

1. The environment variable of the same name.
2. The configuration file.
3. The key's default.

An empty value counts as unset. A required key without a value is an error.

An environment variable that starts with `STORYCREEP_` but is not a key
below is reported as a warning and otherwise ignored.

## The configuration file

The file is optional. Name it with `--config <path>` or with the
`STORYCREEP_CONFIG_FILE` environment variable; the flag wins. It is UTF-8
text of `KEY=value` lines with the key names below:

```sh
# /etc/storycreep/storycreep.env
STORYCREEP_PUBLIC_URL=https://storycreep.example.com
STORYCREEP_SIGNUP=invite
```

- Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored.
- Whitespace around the key and the value is ignored.
- A value wrapped in a matching pair of `"` or `'` is unwrapped.
- Nothing is unescaped or expanded, and a `#` after a value is part of
  the value.
- Every key must be one of the keys below and appear at most once.
  `STORYCREEP_CONFIG_FILE` cannot be set in the file.

This format is simpler than the environment files of Docker Compose
(`env_file`) and systemd (`EnvironmentFile`). A file written for either is
read the same way here only if it has no `export` in front of a key, no comment
after a value, no escape sequence, and no variable reference such as
`${HOME}`. systemd also ignores lines that start with `;` and lines without
an `=`, which are errors here.

## Keys

| Key | Values | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `STORYCREEP_MODE` | `self-hosted`, `hosted` | `self-hosted` | The deployment mode: `self-hosted` for an instance run by its own operator, `hosted` for the operated multi-tenant service. It decides the [capabilities](#capabilities), and no other code reads it. |
| `STORYCREEP_PUBLIC_URL` | An `http` or `https` URL | Required | The URL users open Storycreep at: `http` or `https`, a host name or IP address, and an optional port, with no path. Behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS, it is the proxy's `https` URL, not the address the server listens on. Write an internationalized domain name in its `xn--` (Punycode) form, and an IPv4 address as four decimal numbers. Hosted mode requires `https`. Example: `https://storycreep.example.com`. |
| `STORYCREEP_PUBLIC_SITE` | `on`, `off` | `off` (self-hosted), `on` (hosted) | Whether the instance serves the public site: the marketing pages and the documentation. |
| `STORYCREEP_SIGNUP` | `closed`, `invite`, `open` | Not set | Who can register an account: `closed` (no one), `invite` (people holding an invitation), or `open` (anyone). Not set, self-hosted mode uses the policy that first-run setup chose (PRD FR-ADMIN-02), or `closed` if setup chose none, which the `Signup` capability shows as `setup`; set, it overrides that choice for as long as it is set. Until setup has completed, nobody can register, whatever the policy. Hosted mode always uses `open`, and another value is an error there. |
| `STORYCREEP_INSTANCE_ADMIN_ACCESS` | `on`, `off` | `off` | Whether an instance admin acts as the owner of every workspace and project, without being a member (PRD §5.5): `on` lets them read and manage any workspace, as when its last owner has left, and `off` resolves their role by their memberships, like anyone else's. Hosted mode, where instance admin is restricted to operator accounts, refuses `on`. |
| `STORYCREEP_WORKSPACE_LIMITS` | Limits and whole numbers joined by `=`, separated by commas, such as `members=20, projects=50` | Not set | Caps on what each workspace may use (PRD FR-ENT-01). Self-hosted mode gives every workspace the unlimited plan, so without this key no workspace has a limit. Each entry is a limit and a whole number from 1 to 9007199254740991, joined by `=`: `members`, the most members that a workspace may have, `projects`, the most projects, and `storage_bytes`, the most bytes that its stored files may take up. A limit that the key does not name stays unlimited. A change that would take a workspace past a cap is refused with 409 `limit_exceeded`, whose details name the limit, the workspace's usage, and the cap, and which offers no upgrade. For `members`, which counts guests too, that is accepting an invitation to a workspace that has as many members as the cap allows, `storycreep grant-role`, which then fails, and registering with the link of a link invitation, which any address may register with; registering with the link of an invitation to an address adds the account, which accepts the invitation once a member has left. Inviting someone is not such a change, because it adds no member. For `projects`, it is creating a project, and unarchiving or restoring one, which make it count again. For `storage_bytes`, it is uploading a file that the workspace does not store already, which is refused with 413 `storage_limit_exceeded` instead, with the same details. A workspace that is past a cap already, as after the cap is lowered, keeps what it has, but cannot add more. Hosted mode, where each workspace's plan sets its limits, refuses the key. |
| `STORYCREEP_SMTP_URL` | An `smtp://` or `smtps://` URL | Not set (self-hosted), required (hosted) | The SMTP server that the instance sends its email through (PRD FR-AUTH-03): the links that verify an email address and reset a password. `smtp://` connects with STARTTLS, which the server must offer, on port 587 unless the URL names another port; `smtp://` with `?security=none` sends without TLS, for a relay on the same host or network, and then cannot sign in to it unless its host is `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `::1`; and `smtps://` uses TLS from the start, on port 465 unless the URL names another. A username and a password in the URL, percent-encoded, sign in with PLAIN or LOGIN. With `STORYCREEP_SMTP_FROM`, which it needs, it overrides the SMTP settings that first-run setup chose (PRD FR-ADMIN-02), for as long as it is set. When neither sets a server, the instance sends no email, says so to its users, and an instance admin gives them the links as text instead (`POST /api/v1/admin/password-reset-links`, or `storycreep reset-password`). Hosted mode always sends email (the `EmailRequired` [capability](#capabilities)), so it requires this key. Where the URL is shown, its password is `[REDACTED]`. Example: `smtp://apikey:password@smtp.example.com:587`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SMTP_FROM` | An email address, alone or with a name | Not set (self-hosted), required (hosted) | The address that the instance's email comes from, alone or with a name, with `STORYCREEP_SMTP_URL`, which needs it. The SMTP server must let the instance send from it. Example: `Storycreep <noreply@example.com>`. |
| `STORYCREEP_ASSET_STORAGE` | The absolute path of a directory, or an `s3://` URL | Not set (self-hosted), required (hosted) | Where the instance stores the files of its assets, the images that its users upload (PRD FR-ASSET-01): the absolute path of a directory, for the local driver, or an `s3://` URL of a bucket of an S3-compatible object storage, such as Amazon S3, MinIO, or Cloudflare R2, for the S3 driver. The URL is `s3://access_key_id:secret_access_key@host[:port]/bucket`, with the keys percent-encoded, as `%2F` for `/`, over HTTPS on port 443 unless it names another port, and takes two query parameters: `region`, the bucket's region, `us-east-1` unless it names one, and `security=none` for plain HTTP, on port 80 unless it names another. The bucket must exist, and the keys must let the server read, write, list, and delete its objects; the server addresses it in the path of its URLs, as `https://host/bucket/key`. A file is stored under `{workspace}/{sha256}.{ext}`, the same key in either driver, so switching drivers needs only this key, once the files are copied to the new place with their keys: the server moves none. The local driver serves a file through the API, after it checks the user's access, and the S3 driver through a URL of this host that it signs for 5 minutes, after the same check, which the users' browsers then read the file from. So the host must be one that the browsers reach too, not only the server: a MinIO beside the server needs a host name that both resolve, behind a reverse proxy of its own. A URL of `security=none` is plain HTTP for the browsers too, whose images a page of the application over HTTPS does not load, so it suits only an instance that is itself served over plain HTTP, as on a local network. A client of the API that reads a file with fetch, rather than showing it as an image, needs the bucket's CORS rules to allow GET from `STORYCREEP_PUBLIC_URL`'s origin. Set, the key overrides the bucket that first-run setup chose (PRD FR-ADMIN-02) for as long as it is set; not set, self-hosted mode stores the files in the bucket that setup chose, or else in `/var/lib/storycreep/assets`, which the `BlobDriver` capability shows as `setup`. The directory is created if it does not exist. Hosted mode, which stores no file on the instance's disk, requires an `s3://` URL. The server deletes every file of its workspaces that its own database does not refer to, so two instances never share a bucket: one that runs on a copy of another's database, which names the bucket that setup chose, sets this key to a bucket or a directory of its own. Where the URL is shown, its secret key is `[REDACTED]`. Example: `s3://AKIAEXAMPLE:secret@s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/storycreep?region=eu-central-1`. |
| `STORYCREEP_ASSET_MAX_BYTES` | A whole number from 1 to 52428800 | `10485760` | The largest file, in bytes, that an upload of an asset takes (PRD FR-ASSET-02): a larger one is refused with 413 `request_too_large`. It is at most 52428800 (50 MB), the most that the body of an upload may have (NFR-SEC-07). An SVG file is measured as it was uploaded, before the server removes what it does not allow from it, and then as the server would store it, which may take more bytes, as some of its characters are written as references: one that would then be larger is refused so too. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_OWNER_EMAIL` | An email address | Not set | The email address of the first owner, for unattended first-run setup (PRD FR-ADMIN-02). With `STORYCREEP_SETUP_OWNER_NAME`, `STORYCREEP_SETUP_OWNER_PASSWORD`, and `STORYCREEP_SETUP_WORKSPACE_NAME`, which it needs, it makes the server complete first-run setup itself when it starts on a database whose setup is pending, instead of waiting for someone to complete it with the setup code that it logs. Unattended setup makes the same changes as the setup API: it creates the owner's account, which is an instance admin, and the first workspace, which the owner owns and which is the owner's personal workspace, and records the signup policy of `STORYCREEP_SETUP_SIGNUP`. A value that the setup API would refuse, such as an address that is not one or a weak password, stops the server with an error that names its key, and `storycreep validate-config` reports it too. Once setup has completed, either way, the server ignores these keys. Example: `jo@example.com`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_OWNER_NAME` | A display name | Not set | The display name of the first owner, for unattended first-run setup, which other people see: 1 to 100 characters, not all of them blank, and without control characters. Example: `Jo Novak`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_OWNER_PASSWORD` | A password | Not set | The password of the first owner, for unattended first-run setup: at least 12 characters, and not one of the 10,000 most common passwords. The server reads it only while setup is pending, so remove it from the configuration once setup has completed. Secret: shown as `[REDACTED]`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_WORKSPACE_NAME` | A workspace name | Not set | The name of the first workspace, for unattended first-run setup: 1 to 100 characters, not all of them blank, and without control characters. Its default locale is `STORYCREEP_DEFAULT_LOCALE`. Example: `Harbour Studio`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_WORKSPACE_SLUG` | A slug, such as `harbour-studio` | Not set | The slug of the first workspace, for unattended first-run setup: groups of lowercase ASCII letters and digits joined by single hyphens, of at most 64 characters, and not a reserved word. Not set, it is derived from `STORYCREEP_SETUP_WORKSPACE_NAME`, as the setup API derives it. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_SIGNUP` | `closed`, `invite`, `open` | Not set | The signup policy that unattended first-run setup records, as the setup API's `signup_policy` does: `closed` if it is not set. `STORYCREEP_SIGNUP` overrides it for as long as that is set. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_SMTP_URL` | An `smtp://` or `smtps://` URL | Not set | The SMTP server that unattended first-run setup records, written like `STORYCREEP_SMTP_URL`, as the setup API's `smtp` does, with `STORYCREEP_SETUP_SMTP_FROM`, which it needs. Not set, setup records none, and the instance sends no email unless `STORYCREEP_SMTP_URL` is set, which overrides the recorded server for as long as it is set. The server reads it only while setup is pending, so remove it from the configuration once setup has completed. Where it is shown, its password is `[REDACTED]`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_SMTP_FROM` | An email address, alone or with a name | Not set | The address that the email of the SMTP server of `STORYCREEP_SETUP_SMTP_URL`, which needs it, comes from, written like `STORYCREEP_SMTP_FROM`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SETUP_ASSET_STORAGE` | An `s3://` URL | Not set | The bucket that unattended first-run setup records for the files of the instance's assets, written as an `s3://` URL of `STORYCREEP_ASSET_STORAGE`, as the setup API's `storage` does. Setup records only a bucket: not set, it records none, and the files are stored in `/var/lib/storycreep/assets` unless `STORYCREEP_ASSET_STORAGE` is set, which overrides the recorded bucket for as long as it is set. The server reads it only while setup is pending, so remove it from the configuration once setup has completed. Where it is shown, its secret key is `[REDACTED]`. |
| `STORYCREEP_SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT` | A duration from `5m` to `8760h` (a year), in hours, minutes, and seconds, such as `720h` or `1h30m` | `720h` | How long a session lasts without being used before it ends, and its user must sign in again (PRD FR-AUTH-02). A request made with the session counts as using it, although the server records the use at most once a minute. A change applies to the sessions that exist already, too. |
| `STORYCREEP_SESSION_LIFETIME` | A duration from `5m` to `8760h` (a year), in hours, minutes, and seconds, such as `720h` or `1h30m` | `2160h` | How long a session lasts at most, from when its user signed in, however often it is used (PRD FR-AUTH-02). The session's cookie expires then too. A shorter value applies to the sessions that exist already, too, but a longer one only to those that start after the change, whose cookies are made to last that long. |
| `STORYCREEP_DEFAULT_LOCALE` | A locale that the server has a catalog for: `en` | `en` | The instance's default locale, as a BCP 47 language tag (PRD FR-I18N-02). The server writes its messages, such as those of the API's errors, in the locale that the request's `Accept-Language` header prefers among those that the server has a catalog for, or else in this one. A tag with a region, such as `en-GB`, selects the catalog of that region if the server has one, and else the catalog of its language in the same script, so `zh-TW`, which is written in Traditional Chinese, would not select a `zh` catalog of Simplified Chinese. Only a locale that the server has a catalog for is accepted, so that a mistake is found when the server starts. |
| `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_URL` | A `postgres://` URL | Required | The PostgreSQL database, and the login the server connects to it as: `postgres://user:password@host:port/database`, with the scheme (`postgres` or `postgresql`) in lowercase and characters such as `@`, `:`, `/`, `?`, and `#` in the password percent-encoded. The database server must run PostgreSQL 15 or newer. The login must be an ordinary role with a name of its own: migrations refuse one named `storycreep_app`, `storycreep_definer`, or `storycreep_maintenance`, the roles they create, or starting with `pg_`, which PostgreSQL reserves. The server refuses to use one that is a superuser, has `BYPASSRLS`, `CREATEROLE`, or `REPLICATION`, or owns the database or objects in it, or that is a member of a role that does, of one of the server's privileged roles, or of `pg_execute_server_program`, `pg_read_server_files`, or `pg_write_server_files`, which give access to the database server's files and programs, because row-level security would not hold it, or of `pg_write_all_data`, which may change the rows of every table past what the migrations grant. Migrations create the login if it does not exist, set its password to the one the server logs in with (this URL's, or else the one `PGPASSWORD`, a service file, or a password file supplies), and grant it the `storycreep_app` role. When the server logs in with a password, they refuse a login whose `VALID UNTIL` has passed, which PostgreSQL would refuse as if the password were wrong. They also revoke `CONNECT` on the database from `PUBLIC` and from the server's roles, `storycreep_app`, `storycreep_definer`, and `storycreep_maintenance`, and grant it to the login, to the maintenance login of `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_MAINTENANCE_URL` if that is set, and to the admin login if that took its `CONNECT`, so that no other role can connect unless it is a superuser, or it is, or inherits the privileges of, one of those logins, the database's owner, or a role granted `CONNECT`, as a monitoring role may need to be. They fail if `PUBLIC` or one of the server's roles can still connect afterwards, as through a grant that a role other than the database's owner made, and a server that does not apply migrations itself refuses a migrated database that they can connect to again, as after a dump is restored into a new database, until migrations run again. A login belongs to the whole PostgreSQL server, not to one database, and so does the `storycreep_app` role, which every Storycreep database on the server grants its privileges to. So give each Storycreep database on a server a login of its own, which can connect only to its own database: a shared login would reach all of them, and migrating one would change the password the others log in with. The pool parameters, such as `pool_max_conns`, configure the pool that serves requests. A server that runs the background jobs opens a second pool of the login for them, configured the same way but with at most 8 connections, whatever `pool_max_conns` says. Query parameters, such as `sslmode`, are read as libpq reads them, with an `=` in a value percent-encoded as `%3D`, and the libpq environment variables, such as `PGSSLMODE`, fill in settings the URL leaves out. A space anywhere in the URL is written as `%20`. The URL is checked as the server's connections read it, so a setting they could not use, such as an unknown `sslmode`, a certificate file that cannot be read, or a libpq parameter that they do not support, such as `gssencmode` or `keepalives`, is an error. Where the URL is shown, its password is `[REDACTED]`, and so is the value of every query parameter except the libpq and pgx settings that hold no secret, such as `sslmode`, and `application_name`, `search_path`, `timezone`, and `client_encoding`. Example: `postgres://storycreep:password@db:5432/storycreep`. |
| `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL` | A `postgres://` URL | Not set | A PostgreSQL superuser login for the same database, written like `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_URL`. Only applying migrations uses it, as `storycreep migrate` does. Migrations need a superuser because they create the server's database roles, and one of them bypasses row-level security. It must name a different login from `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_URL`, and the same database. Migrations refuse a login that is, or acts as, `storycreep_app`, `storycreep_definer`, or `storycreep_maintenance`, because they make those roles unable to log in and take `SUPERUSER` away from them. Migrations create the server's tables in the `public` schema, whatever `search_path` this URL, the login, or the database sets. It is shown redacted in the same way. |
| `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_MAINTENANCE_URL` | A `postgres://` URL | Not set | The login of the maintenance jobs, for the same database, written like `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_URL`. The jobs that must see the rows of every workspace, or of workspaces that no longer exist, such as hard deletion and the audit log's retention, work as the `storycreep_maintenance` role, which bypasses row-level security. This login acts as that role, in transactions of its own, which no request uses. It must name a login different from `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_URL` and `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL`, and the same database. When it is set, migrations create the login if it does not exist, set its password as they set the application login's, grant it the `storycreep_maintenance` role, and grant it `CONNECT` on the database, and they refuse a login named like one of the server's roles, or starting with `pg_`, or that could do more than bypass row-level security as `storycreep_maintenance`: one that is a superuser, has `BYPASSRLS` itself, `CREATEROLE`, or `REPLICATION`, owns the database or objects in it, or is a member of a role that does, `storycreep_maintenance` included but for its own `BYPASSRLS`, of `storycreep_app` or `storycreep_definer`, of one of the roles that give access to the database server's files and programs, or of `pg_write_all_data`. Give each Storycreep database on a server a maintenance login of its own, as for `STORYCREEP_DATABASE_URL`. The `storycreep_maintenance` role belongs to the whole PostgreSQL server, and so does its `BYPASSRLS`, so the login could also bypass row-level security in another database on the server that it can connect to, as PostgreSQL lets every role do by default: on a server shared with other applications, revoke `CONNECT` on their databases from `PUBLIC`. Without this URL, migrations leave the maintenance login alone. It is shown redacted in the same way. |
| `STORYCREEP_HTTP_ADDR` | `host:port` or `:port` | `:8080` | The address the server listens on for HTTP: `host:port`, or `:port` for every network interface. The host is an IP address or a host name, and the port a number. It serves the API, the health endpoints `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and `/version`, and everything else except `/metrics`. Behind a reverse proxy, the proxy forwards to this address, and users open `STORYCREEP_PUBLIC_URL`. |
| `STORYCREEP_TRUSTED_PROXIES` | IP addresses and CIDR prefixes, separated by commas, such as `172.18.0.1` or `10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.1.7` | Not set | The reverse proxies in front of the server, whose `X-Forwarded-For` header it believes. The server takes as a request's client the address that its connection comes from, unless that is one of these: then it takes the rightmost address in the request's `X-Forwarded-For` header that is not one of these, because each proxy appends the address that it received the request from, or the leftmost address if every one is. An entry that is not an IP address, such as `unknown`, ends the search, because what lies to its left cannot be checked, and the listed proxy to its right, which wrote it, is taken for the client. The client's address is what the rate limits of an IP address count (PRD NFR-SEC-06), and what a session and the audit log record. Without this setting, behind a reverse proxy, every request seems to come from the proxy, so all clients share the rate limits of one address, which count every request of the API: one client that uses up the limit of signing in refuses everybody's sign-ins until it resets, and one busy client, such as a CI job, that uses up the address's limit of reading or of changing something gets everybody's such requests refused likewise. List only the addresses that the proxies connect from, as the server sees them, because whoever connects from a listed address can claim to be any client. Nor may a listed range hold a client's address, as the proxies see it, such as the addresses of a local network or a VPN that uses the same range: the server skips over every listed address in the header, a client's as well as a proxy's, so that client too can claim to be any client. The proxy must set the header or append to it, as nginx's `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` does, and Caddy and Traefik do unasked. A proxy on the same machine as a container connects to it from the gateway of the container's network, such as `172.18.0.1`, which `docker network inspect` shows, and a proxy in a container from that container's address. |
| `STORYCREEP_ADMIN_ADDR` | `host:port`, `:port`, or `off` | `127.0.0.1:9090` | The address of the admin port, which serves only `/metrics`, in Prometheus's text format, written like `STORYCREEP_HTTP_ADDR`, or `off` for no admin port. Its port must differ from the port of `STORYCREEP_HTTP_ADDR`, unless both name a host, and different ones. The default listens on the loopback interface only, so that only the machine itself can reach it; in a container, set it to `:9090` to let a Prometheus on the container's network scrape it. How `/metrics` answers depends on the `MetricsEndpoint` [capability](#capabilities): `unauthenticated` serves it to anyone who can reach the port, and `protected` only to a request with `STORYCREEP_METRICS_TOKEN` as its bearer token. With `protected` and no token set, there are no metrics, and the admin port is not opened. |
| `STORYCREEP_METRICS_TOKEN` | A token of at least 16 characters | Not set | The bearer token that a scraper sends to `/metrics` on the admin port, in an `Authorization: Bearer` header, when the `MetricsEndpoint` capability is `protected`. Setting it also makes the capability `protected` in self-hosted mode. It is at least 16 characters of letters, digits, and `-._~+/`, optionally followed by `=` characters, as RFC 6750 allows; `openssl rand -hex 32` makes one. Hosted mode protects `/metrics` whether or not it is set, so without it, hosted mode serves no metrics. Secret: shown as `[REDACTED]`. |
| `STORYCREEP_LOG_LEVEL` | `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` | The lowest level that is logged. The record that gives the setup code, which the server writes as a warning at each start while first-run setup is pending (PRD FR-ADMIN-02), is logged whatever the level, because setup cannot complete through the API without the code. |
| `STORYCREEP_CONFIG_FILE` | A file path | Not set | The [configuration file](#the-configuration-file) to read. It is read from the environment only, and `--config` overrides it. |

## Capabilities

`STORYCREEP_MODE` resolves into the capabilities below (PRD §10.3). Code
that behaves differently in the two modes reads a capability, never the mode.
A capability with a key in the last column starts from the mode's value and
can be changed with that key.

| Capability | `self-hosted` | `hosted` | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PublicSite` | `off` | `on` | `STORYCREEP_PUBLIC_SITE` |
| `Signup` | `setup` | `open` | `STORYCREEP_SIGNUP` (self-hosted only) |
| `EnforceEntitlements` | `off` | `on` | — |
| `Billing` | `off` | `on` | — |
| `EmailRequired` | `off` | `on` | — |
| `BlobDriver` | `setup` | `s3` | `STORYCREEP_ASSET_STORAGE` |
| `MetricsEndpoint` | `unauthenticated` | `protected` | `STORYCREEP_METRICS_TOKEN` (`protected` when set) |
| `InstanceAdminUI` | `on` | `operator-only` | — |
| `InstanceAdminAccess` | `off` | `off` | `STORYCREEP_INSTANCE_ADMIN_ACCESS` (self-hosted only) |
| `SSO` | `off` | `plan-feature` | — |
